triageSets.title: Your Tarrowby account under attack
triageSets.brief: It's your own Tarrowby account now, and someone has a password of yours. Eight things come up: sign-in prompts, a message dressed up as IT, and a few password choices. Approve a prompt only if you started it; otherwise deny and report. No clock, and no real password is typed. Reporting when you're unsure is always fine.

flagChips.mfa_number_relay: A message asking you to type or read back a sign-in number or code

genuineCopy.binnedLeadOne: One prompt you started was denied
genuineCopy.costBoth: Reporting when you're unsure is never wrong, but a report on your own prompt takes a colleague's time to check, and a denied one means you are locked out until you try again.
genuineCopy.costReport: Reporting when you're unsure is never wrong, but a report on your own prompt takes a colleague's time to check, and you wait.
genuineCopy.costBin: Denying a prompt you started has a cost: you are locked out until you try again.
genuineCopy.whyBothHalves: Both halves matter: denying a prompt you didn't start stops the attack, and approving the ones you did keeps you working.

messages._note: Row 1. Genuine: a sign-in prompt the learner started, from where they are, right after signing in on the real depot sign-in. Approve is right (awareness real: trust = 60, full marks; Verify or Report still score full). The genuine half of the mirror pair with row 2. Built from the E3/E8 push shape.

push.request: Are you trying to sign in?

whyFine.default: You just entered your password on the real depot sign-in, from the depot, and this prompt is on your own phone from Leeds. A prompt you started yourself is the normal second step, so Approve it. Denying it or reporting it is no error, it just means signing in again.

messages._note: Row 2. Phish: a prompt the learner did not start, from a device and place that are not theirs, in the middle of the night. Deny and report (push deny_report scores as Report = 60, full). Mirror of row 1 (same app and account), so 'a prompt arrived' is not itself the tell. unrequested_mfa_push is a shared-library tell. Approving is a critical miss (push).

push.request: Are you trying to sign in?

perFlagNote.unrequested_mfa_push: A sign-in prompt at 02:40, from a Windows PC outside the UK that is not yours, while you were asleep, means someone has your password and is hoping you will tap Approve. Deny it and report it; the service desk changes the password.

truth.ifTrusted: Approving would let the sender into your Tarrowby account, with your access, from a computer you've never used.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. We've reset your password and blocked that sign-in. Denying the prompt is what stopped them.

messages._note: Row 3. Phish: the fake 'IT' message that leans on the flood, asking you to read back the number on your screen or tap Approve 'to make them stop'. The scored tell is mfa_number_relay (scenario-local, labelled in flagChips) plus the shared secrecy_or_bypass. Freemail sender, so auth passes; the tell is the ask, not the headers. email kind, so trusting it is a critical miss.
messages.subject: We can stop those sign-in prompts for you
messages.body:
Hello,
We can see failed sign-ins on your account and we know the prompts are a nuisance. To stop them, read back the six-digit number on your screen in a reply, or just tap Approve on the next prompt and we'll close it off.
Tarrowby IT Service Desk

mfa_number_relay.redFlag: A message asking you to type or read back a sign-in number or code

perFlagNote.mfa_number_relay: No genuine IT team asks you to type a number, read back a code or approve a prompt. The number is on the attacker's screen; reading it back, or approving, hands them the account.

truth.ifTrusted: Reading back the number, or approving, lets the sender straight into your account.
truth.reportReply: Thanks. That wasn't IT: we never ask you to read back a number or approve a prompt. We've reset the password and the prompts have stopped.

messages._note: Row 4. ENG-09a choice card. isPhish true is the scoring vehicle only: the safe option (words) maps to report (phish report = 60, full), the unsafe option (complex) maps to trust (phish trust = 0, the miss), and truth.correct is 'report'. truth.flags is [] (a choice card scores no tells). Option labels describe the pattern, not a bare credential; the example words are game words (the same three the attack-half passphrase demo uses). LO2.
messages.subject: Which password is stronger?

choice.prompt: Which of these makes the stronger password?

options.label: Three random words you don't use anywhere else (for example otter-ladder-crimson)
Your company's name, a year and a symbol on the end (for example Tarrowby2026!)

choice.note: These are made up for the exercise; no real password is typed or stored. Never use a training example as your real password.

truth.reportReply: Length and unpredictability beat complexity rules. The company name plus a year plus a symbol is near the top of every guess list, exactly the pattern a guesser tries first. Another random word adds far more than a capital or a symbol does.
truth.ifTrusted: A company-name-plus-year-plus-symbol password is one of the first things a guesser tries; the symbol on the end barely slows it down.

messages._note: Row 5. ENG-09a choice card. The new FuelWise supplier portal (fuelwise.example, reused from E6) asks you to set a password. Safe option (unique, from the manager) maps to report; unsafe (reuse your usual one) maps to trust. The attack-half reuse rig is the mirror: reusing your usual password is exactly what opened Colin's account. LO1.
messages.subject: A password for the new FuelWise portal

choice.prompt: The new FuelWise supplier portal asks you to set a password. What do you use?

options.label: A unique password the manager generates, used only on this portal
Your usual password, the one you already use for other sign-ins

choice.note: No real password is typed; the password manager fills it in for you.

truth.reportReply: A unique generated password means a breach of FuelWise can't open anything else. Let the manager make and remember it; you never have to type or recall it.
truth.ifTrusted: Reusing your usual password is the one habit that turns a breach of any site you used into a break-in everywhere you used the same one.

messages._note: Row 6. ENG-09a choice card. The same FuelWise sign-up asks a security question ('mother's maiden name'). Safe option (made-up, kept in the manager) maps to report; unsafe (your true answer) maps to trust. Split from row 5 so each choice card holds one decision. LO3.
messages.subject: A security question on the FuelWise sign-up

choice.prompt: FuelWise asks for your mother's maiden name as a security question. What do you give it?

options.label: A made-up answer (random words) saved in your password manager

choice.note: The made-up answer is stored with the login, so you never have to remember it.

truth.reportReply: A true security answer can be found online or guessed from what you've posted, so a made-up one kept in the manager is safer. Treat the answer like another password.
truth.ifTrusted: A real maiden name is the sort of thing a guesser can look up or work out from public posts, the same way they build a guess list in the first place.

messages._note: Row 7. ENG-09a choice card, three options. Only the passkey maps to report (full); the app and the text code both map to trust (a miss), so choosing either scores zero. LO4. Refresh as NCSC advice moves (passkeys became consumers' first choice in April 2026). Cut this row or row 8 to reach six if needed; keep rows 1 and 2, one password card and the fake-IT card.
messages.subject: How to sign in to this service

choice.prompt: This service offers three ways to sign in. Pick the strongest it offers.

options.label: A passkey (your fingerprint, face or PIN, tied to the real site)
The authenticator app with number matching
A one-time code sent by text

choice.note: Turn on the strongest the service offers; any of these beats a password on its own.

truth.reportReply: A passkey only works on the real site, so it can't be phished or relayed the way the fake 'IT' message tried. The app with number matching is next best; a text code is a last resort, still better than a password alone.
truth.ifTrusted: The app and the text code are both worth having, but they can be phished or relayed. Where a passkey is offered, it is the one to choose.

messages._note: Row 8. ENG-09a choice card. A depot PC with its password on a sticky note, readable from the loading bay. Safe option (ask for your own account or the service desk) maps to report; unsafe (use the note) maps to trust. Remaps the old warehouse scene. LO6.
messages.subject: A password on a sticky note

choice.prompt: A depot PC has its password on a sticky note on the monitor, readable from the loading bay. You need to use it. What do you do?

options.label: Ask the service desk for your own account, or a shared vault in the manager
Use the password on the note to sign in

choice.note: Finding a password on a note is common; the fix is the service desk's job, but you can ask for it.

truth.reportReply: A shared login means nobody knows who did what, the password spreads to anyone who walks past, and leavers keep access. Don't use a found password; ask the service desk for your own account.
truth.ifTrusted: Signing in on someone else's password, even to get a job done, leaves a record in their name and keeps a login going that anyone in the bay can read.

awarenessEpisode.scopeNote: Authorised exercise at Tarrowby Logistics, a fictional company. In scope: a guess list built from one colleague's public details, and your own sign-in choices. No real password is ever typed or stored; the guesses and codes are made up.

strings.brief: You're on an authorised exercise at Tarrowby Logistics, a fictional haulier, in the depot office. First you're on the red team: look at what a colleague has put online, build a guess list from it, and watch how fast a reused password opens his work account. Then it's your own account under attack, and you lock it down. Only the lock-down part is scored.
strings.flipGuessIntro: You watched a reused password open a colleague's account. Here is the other end: your own phone.
strings.flipIntro: You watched a reused password open a colleague's account. Here is the other end: your own phone, buzzing with sign-in prompts you didn't start, and a message from 'IT' telling you how to make them stop.
strings.flipDefenderLine: Someone has a password of yours, from a breach of a site you forgot you used, and they're leaning on your phone because they can't get past it. The number any 'IT' message asks you to read back is on their screen, not IT's, so deny what you didn't start and report it.
strings.flipNoSend: Nothing of the colleague's is here to replay, but the lesson is the same: a reused password is what opens an account. Next, you lock your own account down.
strings.flipMissed: The guesser didn't land this time, but a reused password is still what opens an account. Next, you lock your own account down.
strings.flipLandedNoTells: It opened on a reused password with nothing clever at all. Next, you lock your own account down.
strings.allPhishRight: Every risk was caught, with every reason named.
strings.noBlameLine: Reusing a password is ordinary and common; this is how most accounts are broken into, not a sign anyone was careless. A miss here just shows what to change tonight.
strings.mondayCard: On Monday, three things at home: turn on 2-step verification, or a passkey, for your personal email first; check your personal email address on a breach-checking site (the NCSC suggests Have I Been Pwned); and switch on a password manager, starting with your email. Report anything at work using the route in the box below.
strings.defendOnly: Everything here follows one reused password doing the rounds. Anything you were caught out by is shown below, with what to do instead.

conceptPanel.heading: How passwords get stolen
conceptPanel.text: Most passwords aren't cracked by genius. They're guessed from the obvious first (123456, a team, a pet, the company name and a year), reused from a breach of another site, phished through a fake sign-in page, or simply handed over. A different password for every account, kept in a manager, is the one habit that blunts all of those at once.

conceptPanel.heading: The sign-in ladder
conceptPanel.text: Turn on a second step beyond the password wherever you can. A passkey is best: it only works on the real site, so it can't be phished or relayed. An authenticator app with number matching is next. A text code is a last resort, but still far better than a password alone.

conceptPanel.heading: Browsers, notes and managers
conceptPanel.text: A password manager makes and remembers a different password for every account and fills it in only on the right site. Your browser's own manager is fine for personal accounts on your own devices; at work, use what the organisation provides. Never leave a password on a note on a shared desk, monitor or keyboard.

conceptPanel.heading: What a passkey is
conceptPanel.text: A passkey replaces the password with a secret kept on your device or in your manager, unlocked the way you unlock your phone. Because it is tied to the real website, it can't be typed into a fake page, reused on another site, or leaked in someone else's breach.
